abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a fundamental reconceptualization of test adequacy assessment through the lens of information theory. Traditional coverage-based criteria treat test case selection as a geometric problem, overlooking the semantic diversity of program behaviors. We propose the Information-Theoretic Test Adequacy Framework (ITTAF), which models test suites as information channels and defines adequacy as the maximization of mutual information between test inputs and program state transitions. Our theoretical analysis establishes formal connections between Shannon entropy, branch coverage, and fault detection capability, demonstrating that entropy-based adequacy subsumes existing structural coverage metrics. We prove that ITTAF provides a tighter bound on fault detection probability than any existing coverage criterion under standard fault assumptions. The framework enables a principled approach to test case prioritization based on information gain rather than coverage percentage. Experimental evaluation across 42 subject programs from the SIR benchmark demonstrates that ITTAF-guided test generation achieves statistically significant improvements in fault detection compared to statement coverage, branch coverage, and mutation score. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for test adequacy that unifies structural and functional testing perspectives.

Regression testing remains computationally expensive in modern software development, and selective retest techniques often sacrifice effectiveness for efficiency. This paper presents an enhanced fault-based regression test selection approach that significantly improves both accuracy and scalability over existing methods. Our technique integrates dynamic slicing with incremental program dependence analysis to identify test cases that can safely be excluded while guaranteeing coverage of regression faults. We introduce a novel concept of fault-revealing execution paths that captures the minimal set of program elements affected by code changes. The theoretical analysis proves that our approach achieves completeness guarantees comparable to retest-all while reducing the test suite by an average of 67%. We formalize the relationship between change impact analysis and regression fault localization, demonstrating that our method dominates existing techniques in terms of the theoretical bound on missed faults. Empirical evaluation on 15 industrial software systems with realistic regression scenarios shows that the enhanced approach reduces testing time by 58% on average while maintaining 100% fault detection for all known regression faults. This work substantially advances the theoretical foundations of safe regression test selection.

We introduce DeepTestOracle, a deep learning-based automated test oracle generation system that represents a paradigm shift in software testing practice. Traditional test oracle creation remains a bottleneck requiring extensive manual effort and domain expertise. DeepTestOracle addresses this challenge by training transformer-based models on semantic program embeddings to predict expected outputs for arbitrary test inputs. The system architecture comprises three novel components: (1) a code representation module that captures syntactic and semantic program features, (2) a specification inference engine that learns implicit functional requirements from existing test suites, and (3) an adaptive oracle validation mechanism that quantifies prediction confidence and flags potentially incorrect assertions. Our implementation handles real-world programs with complex I/O operations, including GUI applications and numerical computation software. Evaluation on 200 programs from the Amazon Web Services test corpus demonstrates that DeepTestOracle generates valid test oracles with 94.2% precision and 89.7% recall, successfully automating the oracle generation process for 73% of the evaluated subjects. The system enables continuous integration pipelines to automatically produce comprehensive test suites for previously untested code paths, fundamentally transforming how software testing resources are allocated.

Mutation testing suffers from prohibitive computational costs that limit its practical adoption in industrial settings. We present MuScan-2, a highly optimized mutation testing system that achieves order-of-magnitude performance improvements through innovative algorithmic techniques. The system implements four major architectural enhancements: (1) a parallel mutant execution engine utilizing GPU acceleration for instruction-level mutation evaluation, (2) a learned mutant classification module that predicts equivalent mutants with 91% accuracy, reducing unnecessary executions, (3) a hierarchical mutation clustering strategy that identifies subsuming mutants and avoids redundant evaluations, and (4) an incremental testing framework that reuses test results across mutation campaigns. MuScan-2 introduces the concept of critical mutation coverage, a refined adequacy criterion that prioritizes semantically diverse mutants over syntactically generated variants. The tool supports Java and Python programs with seamless integration into existing build systems. Experimental results on 28 open-source projects show that MuScan-2 reduces average mutation testing time from 4.2 hours to 23 minutes while achieving 98% correlation with traditional mutation scores. An industrial case study at a major telecommunications company demonstrates successful deployment in continuous integration pipelines, enabling daily mutation analysis of million-line codebases.
